Triggers.value: A specific temperature on the skin

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I dwell on how I used to be before the event
I dwell on how the event could have been prevented

Memory.value: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish
When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop

There is something wrong with me as a person
I feel permanently humiliated by what happened

issues.item: Triggers: Olfactory Danger Cue: Burnt smell
issues.explanation: For intimate partner physical abuse, 'being forced to do something' and tactile body-state cues are plausible triggers, but 'burnt smell' introduces a danger cue more typical of fire/explosion trauma and is not supported by the other selected items. It feels disconnected from the stated trauma and the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Fear of Rage: I will not be able to control my anger and will do something terrible
issues.explanation: The appraisal pattern is otherwise self-blaming/defectiveness-focused and tightly linked to triggers, but 'fear of rage' shifts to fear of one's own future violent loss of control. That theme is not supported by the trauma type, the other appraisals, or the maladaptive strategies, making this item difficult to integrate into the same formulation.

issues.item: Memory: Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time; Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
issues.explanation: The memory items indicate highly severe, here-and-now re-experiencing, which is plausible at this PCL-5 level, but they sit awkwardly with the formulation because Memory has only a weak link to Negative Appraisals and no active links to Triggers or Maladaptive Strategies. Selecting two very strong reliving items plus disorganized narration makes Memory appear more central than the formulation suggests.

vignette: Linh, a 35-year-old South Eastern Asian woman and married physical therapist, sought help after years of struggling with her traumatic experiences. Linh had endured severe physical abuse from her romantic partner, an experience that left deep emotional scars and persistent triggers in her daily life. The night of the abuse is still vivid to Linh. She recalls the freezing room, the touch of her abuser’s hands, and the loss of control she felt when being forced into submission. These elements are now potent triggers for Linh; even a slight chill on her skin or an unwanted physical touch can send her spiraling back into that moment. When Linh experiences these triggers at work, such as when patients reach out to her for support, she feels a surge of panic and hypervigilance. She is acutely aware of the potential danger in others’ actions and begins to ruminate on how she could have prevented the event from happening. This past dwelling leads her to question her own agency and strength. Linh’s memory of that night is hauntingly vivid; it feels as though the incident is still ongoing rather than a distant memory. When attempting to recount what happened, Linh often loses track of her thoughts and emotions overwhelm her, making it difficult for her to articulate the experience clearly. This inability to explain her trauma contributes to her sense of being defective and humiliated. She has come to believe that the event occurred because of something she did or failed to do, which reinforces her negative self-appraisals and fuels her ongoing hypervigilance. Linh is certain that there must be something fundamentally wrong with her as a person, and this conviction makes it difficult for her to trust others or feel safe in any situation. The memory of the abuse also exacerbates these negative appraisals; each time she recalls the incident, she feels an overwhelming sense of self-blame and humiliation. This cycle only deepens her hypervigilance and rumination, making it harder for her to function both at work and in her personal life. Linh’s marriage has suffered as a result of these symptoms. Her husband notices that she becomes distant and preoccupied whenever certain triggers occur, leading him to feel increasingly frustrated and concerned. Linh is aware of the strain this places on their relationship but feels helpless to change it without understanding how to cope with her overwhelming reactions. Linh finally sought help when her hypervigilance began to affect her performance at work. She was afraid that she might lose her job if her condition worsened, and more importantly, she feared never finding a way to reclaim control over her life. What frightened her most was the thought of living in perpetual fear and feeling permanently damaged by her past. Linh hopes for a chance to heal and regain a sense of normalcy, both in her professional life as a physical therapist and within her marriage. She is determined to break free from the cycle that has held her captive since the traumatic event.
